title: Factors influencing the quality of fruit crops during harvest and post-harvest
competency: Explain how harvest stage, time and method and postharvest handling affect fruit quality.

keywords.def: The stage of development at which fruit is picked; it decides quality and storage life.
Cooling fruit to storage temperature immediately after harvest.
Separating fruit by size and quality level.
Damage from long exposure to low, non-freezing temperatures; it affects tropical fruits.

en.text: The stage of harvest, the time of harvest and the harvesting method all affect fruit quality. Maturity at harvest is one of the main factors that decide a fruit's composition and storage life. Many fruits reach peak eating quality when fully ripe on the tree, but they are usually picked when nearly ripe; some, like avocado, only ripen after picking.

screens.title: Ripe on the tree?
screens.ask: Avocados can hang on the tree for weeks and stay hard. When do they soften?
screens.after: Avocado does not ripen on the tree; it softens after harvest. Not every fruit is best ripened on the tree.

paras: Consider the stage, the time and the method of harvest.

en.text: After harvest, fruit for longer storage is pre-cooled to storage temperature at once, then sorted and graded by size and quality and packed in materials that reduce moisture loss. It is cleaned of soil, dirt and insect waste before storage, kept at the right low temperature with relative humidity above 90%, and handled carefully in transport because mechanical injuries promote disease. Temperate fruits store near 0 °C, but tropical fruits need about 10–13 °C to avoid chilling injury.

screens.title: Which store is colder?
screens.ask: Should apples or bananas be stored at the colder temperature?
screens.after: Apples keep well near 0 °C. Bananas get chilling injury below about 13 °C.

screens.title: Postharvest considerations
paras: Pre-cooling: cool fruit to storage temperature right after harvest.
Sorting and grading: by size and quality level.
Packaging: materials should reduce moisture loss.
Storage: clean off soil, dirt and insect waste first.
Relative humidity above 90% limits water loss.
Transport: handle carefully. Mechanical injuries promote disease.

screens.title: The right temperature
paras: The book says "around freezing point" for most fruits.
That is right for temperate fruits: apple, pear, grape near 0 °C.
Tropical fruits suffer chilling injury there.
Use the lowest SAFE temperature for each fruit.

notes.text: p.39: "Nearly all fruits reach peak eating quality fully ripened on the tree" — avocado does not ripen on the tree, and pears and bananas are better picked mature-green. The lesson says "many fruits".

p.39–40: "temperatures around freezing point" suits temperate fruits only; tropical fruits get chilling injury below about 10–13 °C (banana ≈ 13 °C, mango ≈ 10–13 °C). Recommended RH is usually 85–95%; the book says >90%.
